tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the minimum bridge from the low-pass differential equation to the frequency-response method: assume a sinusoidal input/output pair and use the fact that differentiation of $e^{j\omega t}$ produces a $j\omega$ factor.

sections.section_title: Replacing Low-Pass Derivatives with \(j\omega\) Factors

sections.section_title: Identifying $RC$ as the Cutoff-Setting Quantity
sections.learning_goal: Use the inverse cutoff formula to decide whether two RC filters share the same cutoff and identify which component change matters.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the comparison is symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example text-only; the comparison uses only $RC$ products and cutoff formulas.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct symbolic answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask whether two RC component pairs have the same cutoff frequency or which pair has the lower cutoff.
distractor_plan: Treat $R$ alone as controlling the cutoff.
Treat $C$ alone as controlling the cutoff.
Reverse the inverse relationship and claim larger $RC$ gives a higher cutoff.
Claim the cutoff cannot be determined from $RC$ alone.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Briefly restate that cutoff depends only on the product $RC$, then move straight into the comparison.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Compare two component pairs with the same product $RC$.
paragraph_plan: State the two component pairs.
Compute each $RC$ product.
Substitute into $\omega_c = 1/RC$ and compare the cutoff frequencies.
Conclude that equal $RC$ gives equal transition location.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Two RC low-pass filters have $(R,C) = (1\,\text{k}\Omega, 1\,\mu\text{F})$ and $(R,C) = (2\,\text{k}\Omega, 0.5\,\mu\text{F})$. Determine whether they have the same cutoff frequency and identify the controlling quantity.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute both products, substitute into $\omega_c = 1/RC$, and conclude that equal products give the same cutoff.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the intro rule from a formula statement to a concrete comparison of two RC values.
solution_step_plan: Compute $R_1C_1$ and $R_2C_2$.
Use $\omega_c = 1/RC$ to compare the cutoff frequencies.
State that the cutoff is the same because the products match.
Connect the result back to the transition location of the magnitude response.
practice_variation_axes: Change one component while holding the product $RC$ fixed.
Ask whether two filters have the same cutoff or which one is lower.
Swap low-pass and high-pass labels without changing the cutoff rule.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the comparison symbolic and test the inverse relationship, not the circuit derivation.

sections.section_title: Predicting a Low-Pass Magnitude Response After Changing $RC$
sections.learning_goal: Predict how changing $RC$ moves the low-pass cutoff and shifts the magnitude-response transition left or right.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the low-pass shift is determined from $RC$ and the cutoff formula.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example symbolic; no graph is required because the shift is read from the cutoff formula.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct symbolic answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask how doubling or halving $RC$ changes the low-pass cutoff and where the transition shifts.
distractor_plan: Claim the cutoff increases when $RC$ increases.
Claim the magnitude-response transition shifts to the right when $RC$ increases.
Confuse the low-pass response with a high-pass response.
Say the response is unchanged because only the filter type matters.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Re-anchor the low-pass example in $\omega_c = 1/RC$ and make the direction of the shift explicit before the worked example begins.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from one low-pass response and a factor change in $RC$.
paragraph_plan: Restate the low-pass cutoff formula.
Apply the factor change to $RC$.
Convert the new product back to $\omega_c$.
Interpret the result as a left or right shift in the magnitude-response transition.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A low-pass filter has cutoff $\omega_c = 1/RC$. If $RC$ doubles, determine the new cutoff frequency and state how the magnitude-response transition shifts relative to the original curve.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that doubling $RC$ halves the cutoff frequency and shifts the low-pass transition to lower frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Applies the same inverse rule to a changed low-pass response instead of comparing two component pairs.
solution_step_plan: Write the original cutoff formula.
Apply the factor change to the product $RC$.
Compute the new cutoff as half the original value.
Interpret the shift as moving the transition left on the frequency axis.
practice_variation_axes: Use doubling, halving, or tripling of $RC$.
Ask about a fixed test frequency relative to the old and new cutoffs.
Ask whether the magnitude at a frequency is more or less attenuated after the change.

sections.handoff_notes: The practice should stay focused on cutoff shift direction and low-pass transition location.

sections.section_title: Predicting a High-Pass Magnitude Response After Changing $RC$
sections.learning_goal: Predict how changing $RC$ moves the high-pass cutoff and changes whether a test frequency lies nearer the passband or attenuation region.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the high-pass shift is determined from $RC$ and the cutoff formula.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example symbolic; no graph is required because the shift is read from the cutoff formula.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct symbolic answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask how doubling or halving $RC$ changes the high-pass cutoff and whether a frequency moves closer to the passband.
distractor_plan: Claim the cutoff increases when $RC$ increases.
Reverse the high-pass interpretation and say a lower cutoff makes the signal more attenuated.
Confuse high-pass behavior with low-pass behavior.
Say the transition location stays fixed.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Re-use $\omega_c = 1/RC$ for the high-pass case and make the passband interpretation explicit before the worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from one high-pass response and a factor change in $RC$.
paragraph_plan: Restate the high-pass cutoff formula.
Apply the factor change to $RC$.
Compute the new cutoff frequency.
Interpret the result in terms of passband proximity and attenuation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A high-pass filter has cutoff $\omega_c = 1/RC$. If $RC$ doubles, determine the new cutoff frequency and say whether a frequency just below the original cutoff is closer to or farther from the passband.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that doubling $RC$ halves the cutoff frequency and moves the transition to lower frequency, making the same test frequency less deeply attenuated relative to the old cutoff.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the same inverse cutoff rule, but interprets the opposite side of the magnitude response.
solution_step_plan: Write the cutoff formula for the high-pass filter.
Apply the factor change to $RC$ and compute the new cutoff.
Compare the fixed frequency to the old and new cutoffs.
State how the passband or attenuation interpretation changes.
practice_variation_axes: Use frequencies below or above the original cutoff.
Increase or decrease $RC$ by a factor.
Ask whether the test frequency becomes more or less attenuated.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the distinction from the low-pass example explicit: the cutoff rule is the same, but the response interpretation changes.

sections.section_title: Comparing Magnitude-Response Transitions for Different $RC$ Values
sections.learning_goal: Compare low-pass and high-pass transition locations for two different $RC$ values and identify which curve moves to the lower frequency.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the comparison is symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the comparison text-only; the only required reasoning is the ordering of $RC$ and the cutoff frequency.

question_policy.answer_format: Five-choice multiple-choice with one correct symbolic answer.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which of two RC filters has the lower cutoff and whether the low-pass and high-pass transitions move the same way.
distractor_plan: Reverse the cutoff ordering for the two $RC$ values.
Say only the low-pass cutoff shifts with $RC$.
Say only the high-pass cutoff shifts with $RC$.
Claim larger $RC$ raises the cutoff instead of lowering it.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Set up a comparison of two different $RC$ values and make the shared left-shift rule for both filter types explicit.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Compare two filters with $RC_1 < RC_2$ so the cutoff ordering is unambiguous.
paragraph_plan: State the ordering of the two $RC$ values.
Convert that ordering into the cutoff ordering with $\omega_c = 1/RC$.
Apply the same ordering to both low-pass and high-pass transition locations.
Summarize that larger $RC$ means lower cutoff for both filter types.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Two RC filters satisfy $RC_1 < RC_2$. Compare their cutoff frequencies and magnitude-response transition locations for both the low-pass and high-pass responses.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the larger product $RC_2$ gives the lower cutoff frequency and that both filter types shift their transitions to lower frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Synthesizes the shared rule across both filter types instead of one response at a time.
solution_step_plan: Compare $RC_1$ and $RC_2$ directly.
Convert the comparison into cutoff ordering with $\omega_c = 1/RC$.
State the transition ordering for the low-pass response.
State the transition ordering for the high-pass response.
Summarize the shared conclusion for both filter types.
practice_variation_axes: Change the ratio between the two $RC$ values.
Ask for the ordering of the cutoffs rather than the exact numbers.
Ask for a single statement that applies to both low-pass and high-pass responses.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this final comparison to lock in the shared rule that larger $RC$ lowers the cutoff for both filter types.
